headline_marked: [[Soft Memory Extends Context Length]], Gives 4 Speedups
headline: Soft Memory Extends Context Length, Gives 4 Speedups
summary: MemFold's soft memory technique doubles the usable user history for AI models while dramatically cutting inference overhead. It compresses long dialogues into fixed-size latent vectors, allowing models to handle up to 128K tokens without increased input footpr
details: MemFold introduces a fixed-budget soft memory that doubles the amount of user history an AI model can effectively use. This innovation also dramatically cuts inference overhead by compressing arbitrarily long dialogues into a handful of latent vectors. The model then processes these vectors as ordinary tokens, avoiding the need to process the full raw transcript.

Traditional methods for extending context length involved either feeding increasingly longer token streams, which quickly exhausts GPU memory, or scattering retrieval calls throughout the prompt, adding latency and often hindering reasoning. These approaches treat memory as engineering hacks that scale linearly with history length, rather than a learnable interface.

MemFold's soft memory is truly size-agnostic, with its size independent of the history length. By fixing a budget of 256 continuous vectors, the system can scale from 32K to 128K tokens of raw history without increasing the model’s input footprint, offering significant efficiency gains.

On the accuracy front, the method achieves the highest accuracy across all tested benchmarks and backbones, tying the strongest baseline in one PrefEval cell. This demonstrates that the compressed representation does not compromise task performance, even as the context length grows substantially.

The technique also significantly reduces inference cost. Authors report that the average end-to-end cost remains close to full-context inference and is lower in aggregate for all three tested backbones. This indicates that the additional memory module adds negligible runtime while delivering faster overall predictions.

However, the paper leaves some questions open, such as scaling beyond the fixed 256-vector soft-memory budget, which may require redesign. The on-policy optimization and confidence-gated distillation methods, while effective, introduce an extra training phase with a frozen teacher model, potentially cumbersome for teams with limited compute resources.

Despite these points, the method shows promising transferability to domains like open-ended generation and code completion, beyond its primary persona-driven benchmarks. If these results generalize, MemFold could establish a new baseline for long-context benchmarks, enabling production assistants to double usable context without requiring larger GPUs.

topic: nyc click to cancel rule in effect
headline_marked: [[NYC's 'Click to Cancel' rule]] is finalized, takes effect October 2026
headline: NYC's 'Click to Cancel' rule is finalized, takes effect October 2026
summary: The new municipal rule requires businesses to offer one-click cancellation for subscriptions if they allow one-click sign-up, protecting consumers from difficult cancellation processes. Enforcement begins October 1, 2026.
details: New York City has finalized its 'Click to Cancel' rule, requiring businesses to provide a simple, one-click cancellation process for subscriptions if they offer one-click sign-up. This groundbreaking municipal regulation aims to protect consumers from frustrating and time-consuming hurdles when trying to end unwanted services.

The rule, a first-in-the-nation initiative, specifically targets 'subscription traps' where companies make it intentionally difficult for customers to cancel. It ensures that the ease of signing up is matched by the ease of opting out.

Enforcement of the 'Click to Cancel' rule will begin on October 1, 2026, by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP). Businesses found in violation face civil penalties starting at $525 and may be required to refund affected consumers.

Consumers who experience difficulties canceling subscriptions after the rule takes effect can file complaints with the DCWP. The department provides channels for submitting complaints via mail or fax, along with supporting documentation.
